message.content:
You are investigating a Go codebase at /bench/repo (project name "memos" in codebase-memory-mcp). Answer these two questions with full evidence:

**h06**: Which RPC handler methods can transitively cause an outbound HTTP request to a user-configured URL? Name at least three, and the single function where those paths converge before delivery.

**h07**: Trace how a browser's request for another user's profile image reaches stored data: the serving handler and each hop to the data layer, with files.

For h06: Look at webhook delivery or notification systems. Trace which RPC/API handlers trigger webhooks or outbound HTTP calls. Find the convergence function.

For h07: Look for profile image/avatar serving. Trace from HTTP handler through service layer to data/storage layer.

Report specific file paths and line numbers for all findings.

- codebase-memory: Use the codebase knowledge graph for structural code queries. Triggers on: explore the codebase, understand the architecture, what functions exist, show me the structure, who calls this function, what does X call, trace the call chain, find callers of, show dependencies, impact analysis, dead code, unused functions, high fan-out, refactor candidates, code quality audit, graph query syntax, Cypher query examples, edge types, how to use search_graph.
- dataviz: Use this skill whenever you are about to create ANY chart, graph, plot, dashboard, or data visualization, in ANY output medium — an HTML or React artifact, inline SVG, plotting code in any library (matplotlib, plotly, d3, Recharts, …), an image/PNG you will render and upload, or a chart shared into Slack. Read it BEFORE writing the first line of chart code, choosing chart colors, building a stat tile / meter / KPI row, or laying out a dashboard. Produces visualizations that read as one system — elegant, accessible, consistent in light and dark — using a brand-neutral placeholder palette you swap for your own. Teaches a design-system-agnostic method: a form heuristic, a color formula with a runnable validator, mark specs, and interaction rules. A validated default palette is documented in `references/palette.md` — swap that file's values for your brand's. Triggers on: "chart", "graph", "plot", "data viz", "visualization", "dashboard", "analytics", "visualize data", "categorical colors", "sequential / diverging palette", "stat tile", "sparkline", "heatmap", "legend", "axis", "tooltip", "chart colors", "color by series".
- update-config: Use this skill to configure the Claude Code harness via settings.json. Automated behaviors ("from now on when X", "each time X", "whenever X", "before/after X") require hooks configured in settings.json - the harness executes these, not Claude, so memory/preferences cannot fulfill them. Also use for: permissions ("allow X", "add permission", "move permission to"), env vars ("set X=Y"), hook troubleshooting, or any changes to settings.json/settings.local.json files. Examples: "allow npm commands", "add bq permission to global settings", "move permission to user settings", "set DEBUG=true", "when claude stops show X". For simple settings like theme/model, suggest the /config command.
- keybindings-help: Use when the user wants to customize keyboard shortcuts, rebind keys, add chord bindings, or modify ~/.claude/keybindings.json. Examples: "rebind ctrl+s", "add a chord shortcut", "change the submit key", "customize keybindings".
- simplify: Review the changed code for reuse, simplification, efficiency, and altitude cleanups, then apply the fixes. Quality only — it does not hunt for bugs; use /code-review for that.
- fewer-permission-prompts: Scan your transcripts for common read-only Bash and MCP tool calls, then add a prioritized allowlist to project .claude/settings.json to reduce permission prompts.
- loop: Run a prompt or slash command on a recurring interval (e.g. /loop 5m /foo, defaults to 10m) - When the user wants to set up a recurring task, poll for status, or run something repeatedly on an interval (e.g. "check the deploy every 5 minutes", "keep running /babysit-prs"). Do NOT invoke for one-off tasks.
- claude-api: Reference for the Claude API / Anthropic SDK — model ids, pricing, params, streaming, tool use, MCP, agents, caching, token counting, model migration.
TRIGGER — read BEFORE opening the target file; don't skip because it "looks like a one-liner" — whenever: the prompt names Claude/Anthropic in any form (Claude, Anthropic, Fable, Opus, Sonnet, Haiku, `anthropic`, `@anthropic-ai`, `claude-*`, `us.anthropic.*`, `[1m]`); the user asks about an LLM (pricing/model choice/limits/caching) — never answer from memory; OR the task is LLM-shaped with provider unstated (agent/MCP/tool-definition/multi-agent/RAG/LLM-judge/computer-use; generate/summarize/extract/classify/rewrite/converse over NL; debugging refusals/cutoffs/streaming/tool-calls/tokens).
SKIP only when another provider is being worked on (overrides all triggers): OpenAI/GPT/Gemini/Llama/Mistral/Cohere/Ollama named in the query; OR `grep -rE 'openai|langchain_openai|google.generativeai|genai|mistralai|cohere|ollama'` over the project hits (run this grep FIRST if no provider named — don't Read the file).
- run: Launch and drive this project's app to see a change working. Use when asked to run, start, or screenshot the app, or to confirm a change works in the real app (not just tests). First looks for a project skill that already covers launching the app; otherwise falls back to built-in patterns per project type (CLI, server, TUI, Electron, browser-driven, library).

- review: Review a GitHub pull request; for your working diff use /code-review
- security-review: Complete a security review of the pending changes on the current branch

## h06: RPC handler methods that transitively cause outbound HTTP requests to a user-configured URL

### The convergence function

All outbound HTTP delivery converges on a single function:

**`webhook.Post`** in `/bench/repo/internal/webhook/webhook.go`, line 120.

This function constructs an HTTP POST request to the user-configured `requestPayload.URL` (line 126), optionally signs it with HMAC-SHA256 using the user's signing secret, and sends it via `safeClient.Do(req)` (line 152).

Every caller reaches `Post` through `webhook.PostAsync` (`/bench/repo/internal/webhook/webhook.go`, line 184), which enqueues the payload onto `asyncPostQueue`. The `init()` function (line 42) runs 4 goroutine workers that dequeue and call `Post`.

### RPC handler methods that transitively trigger outbound HTTP

There are at least **six** RPC handlers; here are the required three-plus:

1. **`CreateMemo`** (`/bench/repo/server/router/api/v1/memo_service.go`, line 70)
   - Calls `s.DispatchMemoCreatedWebhook()` at line 157
   - Which calls `s.dispatchMemoRelatedWebhook()` with activity type `"memos.memo.created"` (`memo_service_webhooks.go`, line 16)
   - Which calls `webhook.PostAsync()` (`memo_service_webhooks.go`, line 71)
   - Which funnels to `webhook.Post()` (`webhook.go`, line 46)

2. **`DeleteMemo`** (`/bench/repo/server/router/api/v1/memo_service.go`, line 518)
   - Calls `s.DispatchMemoDeletedWebhook()` at line 562
   - Which calls `s.dispatchMemoRelatedWebhook()` with activity type `"memos.memo.deleted"` (`memo_service_webhooks.go`, line 26)
   - Which calls `webhook.PostAsync()` -> `webhook.Post()`

3. **`UpdateMemo`** (`/bench/repo/server/router/api/v1/memo_service.go`, line 401)
   - Calls `s.dispatchMemoUpdatedSideEffects()` at line 513
   - Which calls `s.DispatchMemoUpdatedWebhook()` (`memo_update_helpers.go`, line 67)
   - Which calls `s.dispatchMemoRelatedWebhook()` with activity type `"memos.memo.updated"` (`memo_service_webhooks.go`, line 21)
   - Which calls `webhook.PostAsync()` -> `webhook.Post()`

4. **`CreateMemoComment`** (`/bench/repo/server/router/api/v1/memo_service_comments.go`, line 20)
   - Calls `s.DispatchMemoCommentCreatedWebhook()` at line 119
   - Which directly calls `webhook.PostAsync()` (`memo_service_webhooks.go`, line 43)
   - Also transitively calls `CreateMemo` (which dispatches `memo.created` webhook)

5. **`SetMemoRelations`** (`/bench/repo/server/router/api/v1/memo_relation_service.go`, line 16)

All six handlers pass through **`webhook.Post`** (`/bench/repo/internal/webhook/webhook.go`, line 120). ## h07: How a browser's request for another user's profile image reaches stored data

### Route registration

The avatar route is registered in `/bench/repo/server/router/fileserver/fileserver.go`, line 124:
```
fileGroup.GET("/users/:identifier/avatar", s.serveUserAvatar)
```

A browser hits: `GET /file/users/{username}/avatar`

### Hop-by-hop trace

**Hop 1: HTTP Handler -- `serveUserAvatar`**
- File: `/bench/repo/server/router/fileserver/fileserver.go`, lines 167-210
- Extracts `:identifier` param (the username) from the URL (line 183)
- On private instances, authenticates the viewer via `s.getCurrentUser()` (line 174, which calls `s.authenticator.AuthenticateToUser()` at line 711 in the same file)
- Calls `s.getUserByUsername(ctx, identifier)` (line 185)

**Hop 2: FileServer helper -- `getUserByUsername`**
- File: `/bench/repo/server/router/fileserver/fileserver.go`, lines 715-717
- Delegates to `s.Store.GetUser(ctx, &store.FindUser{Username: &identifier})`

**Hop 3: Store layer -- `Store.GetUser`**
- File: `/bench/repo/store/user.go`, lines 148-169
- Checks the in-memory user cache by ID (line 150); since the lookup is by username (not ID), the cache is bypassed
- Calls `s.ListUsers(ctx, find)` (line 158)

**Hop 4: Store layer -- `Store.ListUsers`**
- File: `/bench/repo/store/user.go`, lines 136-146
- Delegates to the database driver: `s.driver.ListUsers(ctx, find)` (line 137)
- The `Driver` interface is defined at `/bench/repo/store/driver.go`, line 47

**Hop 5: Database driver -- `DB.ListUsers` (SQLite implementation)**
- File: `/bench/repo/store/db/sqlite/user.go`, line 88
- Builds a SQL query with `WHERE username = ?` (line 129) when `find.Username` is set
- The `SELECT` includes the `avatar_url` column (line 159)
- Scans the result into a `store.User` struct, populating `AvatarURL` (a `string` field at `/bench/repo/store/user.go`, line 43)

**Hop 6: Back in `serveUserAvatar` -- data URI parsing**
- File: `/bench/repo/server/router/fileserver/fileserver.go`, lines 192-209
- Checks `user.AvatarURL == ""` (line 192); returns 404 if no avatar
- Calls `s.parseDataURI(user.AvatarURL)` (line 196), which uses a regex to extract MIME type and base64-decode the image bytes (lines 737-750)
- Validates the MIME type against `avatarAllowedTypes` (line 201; allowed types at lines 75-83)
- Sets security headers and returns the decoded binary blob: `c.Blob(http.StatusOK, imageType, imageData)` (line 209)

### Key insight about data storage

Avatars are stored as **data URIs** (base64-encoded inline) directly in the `avatar_url` column of the `user` table in the database. There is no separate file or object storage for avatars -- the image bytes are embedded in the user record itself. The `parseDataURI` method (line 737) decodes `data:image/png;base64,iVBOR...` format strings back into raw bytes for serving.
